### Results record the runner's machine name, and the installer provides jsonschema

[`89c88701e12f`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/89c88701e12f93c747b40bef7c16d1ecc012c8ff) · [log `747b5ba7f4cc`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/353e094e-5bc2-42ab-966c-b858752c38d6/747b5ba7f4cc53bef8e6f2d5f0198925a99c171f6697d5023e4f13c72676d864.jsonl.gz)

A new runner setting, machine_name (verification/pipeline.toml, empty by default; set per machine in pipeline.local.toml), is what a result records as runner.host and environment.host, and what the note in a truncated log names, in place of the hostname. This lets machines be aliased as more VMs or cloud runners are added, without publishing hostnames, which the trace redactor already treats as personal. Claims in the runner's local state keep the real hostname, which they need to recognise their own stale claims. The VM now running the queue is named vm-1 in its local config; results from the WSL laptop keep its hostname, FilSurface, as before.

The first run on the VM failed 26 of its first 50 jobs within a second, all because the Python module jsonschema was missing: build.py publishes no example result it cannot validate. The Ubuntu installer now installs python3-jsonschema and doctor.sh checks it. Verified: the pipeline's unit tests pass (23, with a new test that a configured machine name is recorded in both host fields and the truncated-log note, and the hostname nowhere in the result); doctor.sh reports jsonschema 4.19.2 on the VM.

### The verification runner stops a step past its timeout only when it has stalled; the installer puts GNU coreutils first on Ubuntu 26.04

[`ad20a5d13d27`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/ad20a5d13d272d76fe74a7ed54b62ff495783ef7) · [log `7d5e20954251`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/353e094e-5bc2-42ab-966c-b858752c38d6/7d5e20954251764c22c4c405e391d57c172a884b13002f302f1c281c941cb3fd.jsonl.gz)

A job's timeout used to be a deadline: at 4 times its estimate (at least 5 minutes) a step was stopped, working or not. Estimates are often far off, and a long run is information about the change and the machine, so the timeout is now where the runner starts looking for a hang. Past it, a step is stopped only once it has stalled: under 1% of a CPU (read from its cgroup, or from /proc for its session without one) and no new log output for stall_window, 10 minutes by default. A step still working is left to finish, and the result marks it overranTimeout with an attention line. Only max_timeout (6h by default) stops a step that is still working; stoppedFor says which rule stopped one. Results record both settings.

Ubuntu 26.04 ships the Rust uutils as its coreutils, and jobs noticed: timeout exits 124 rather than GNU's 137 after -s KILL, which failed the job for example 142 killed mid-proof. build-essential depends on coreutils-from-uutils there, so the installer does not switch system-wide; it links GNU's gnu-prefixed binaries under their own names into ~/.local/lib/gnu-coreutils and puts that first on PATH in .bashrc, .profile (a non-interactive login shell stops early in .bashrc) and .zshrc. doctor.sh fails when timeout is not GNU's, and every result now records the coreutils its job saw.

### Verification findings that need a person go into verification/findings.md, kept by the agent that runs the pipeline

change `uqpqmzoxzroo` · [log `ce943dd82f8a`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/353e094e-5bc2-42ab-966c-b858752c38d6/ce943dd82f8a5f95713a1f1485d6371f150e11375652ba738a3de814226a891c.jsonl.gz)

A run's findings lived in its results, its commit message and the managing session's report, and the last two are easy to lose before anyone acts. verification/findings.md is now the durable list: each entry (VF-NNN) records a verdict against a change, an error a submitter must fix, or a decision that changes what the results mean, with its jobs, commit and machine, what was found, what would settle it and who should act, where else it is tracked, and the check that closes it. Open entries come first.

It starts with the two open findings from the first runs on vm-1: VF-001, the conformance corpus jobs where JBMC proves claims the JVM refutes, reports violations the JVM does not reproduce, and --engine auto passes JBMC's wrong Verified through (Phase 1 of the sound-verdicts brief is not done); and VF-002, examples 147-149, whose patches create their subject file, which build.py's excerpts() does not accept. The run-verification skill gains a Record step (add, update, close; never close on a job that did not run the named check), reads open entries before a run, commits the file with the results and names entries in its report. The unattended verification loop's instruction and the verification README say the same.

### 2. 2026-11-06 16:57 UTC

> This is all working as designed, we may upgrade setup later but for now the missing capabilities are not needed. Let's try to publish Cloudflare logs next (unless this happened as part of push, then do nothing). After that, let's review run-verification -- I would like to run all the verification jobs on this machine. Its config designed for a much weaker system. Ensure that Claude Code has a good amount of memory for loops (like 8GB, in case experiments are run), then you can dedicate whatever else VM does not need to running verification jobs more efficiently.

**Reply:**

The runner picked up the new budget: 12 workers, 24 CPUs, 32 GiB, at most 14 GiB per job, each step capped in its own systemd scope. Only 5 jobs started at first. That's because a job that needs a fresh jvmcontract build reserves the 6 GiB build allowance instead of its own memory limit. Once the builds are cached, more jobs can run at once.

**What I did:**
- **Cloudflare logs:** nothing needed. The earlier push had already uploaded them, and `check --remote` confirms every log is live on the CDN with 0 errors.
- **8 GB for Claude Code loops:** I added `export FEATURE_LOOP_MEMORY_MAX=8G` to `~/.profile`. It applies to new login shells, so start any loop from a new SSH session, or prefix the command with `FEATURE_LOOP_MEMORY_MAX=8G`. Only one feature loop can run at a time, because it always uses the same systemd scope name.
- **Runner budget** (`verification/pipeline.local.toml`, which is machine-local and not committed): the existing file allowed 6 workers, 22 CPUs and 30G. I raised it to 12 workers, 24 CPUs and 32G. Of the 46 GiB, that leaves 8G for a loop, about 2G for the OS, Docker and interactive sessions, and about 4G spare, since the VM has no swap. Jobs ask for only 1–2 CPUs each, so the old worker count, not memory, was holding the runner back. I also corrected that file's comment, which wrongly said up to four loops could run at once.

## Performance compared with the WSL laptop

| | WSL (FilSurface) | VM (vm-1) |
|---|---|---|
| Jobs at once | 2 | up to 12 |
| 57 jobs | ~3.5 h of runner time, at estimates | **7.2 min elapsed** (24 job-minutes) |

Most of the gain comes from running jobs side by side, not from faster steps. Each individual step is roughly as fast as on WSL; it depends on the kind of work. I compared the same example's step on both machines, leaving out any step that reused earlier work:

| Kind of work | Steps | VM speed relative to WSL (wall time) | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| B8 / B9 / B11 (short JBMC and own-checker runs, 2–35 s) | 19 | **0.55–0.8× (slower)** | CPU time is higher too, so the laptop's cores are faster at short JVM-bound runs |
| D1, long TLC runs (101: 316→215 s, 104: 606→402 s) | 2 | **~1.5× faster** | The only fair comparison on long-running work |
| D1, short TLC runs | 4 | about the same | |
| B12, Gradle (81–116 s → 10–20 s) | 3 | ~7× faster, **but don't trust it** | CPU time fell about 11×, so Gradle almost certainly skipped work using caches the first run warmed up |

## Findings for the people who wrote the jobs
1. **Conformance corpus (jobs `20261106-021741` and `20261106-024336`):** both fail on real disagreements with the JVM, which is what they were written to catch.
   - In the plain JBMC mode (`--gaps strict`), JBMC reports *Verified* for `capacity`, `builderCapacity`, `mapCapacity`, `setCapacity` and `loadFactor`, but running them on a real JVM disproves those claims. That is unsound and the most serious finding of the run.
